introduction: One figure runs through all these readings: the soul is soil, the word of God is seed and rain, and the teacher, or God himself, is the farmer who ploughs, weeds, waters and waits. Some passages stress the labour of cultivation, some the readiness of the ground, some the sapling that has begun to grow, and the last are prayers spoken by the seed. The figure is among the oldest in scripture, and the parables of the sower and the fig tree, Isaiah's rain, Paul's planting and watering and the Qur’an's sown corn are set beside the readings, with Mencius, Herbert and Voltaire. The contrasts ask whose work the garden is, whether any ground is beyond help, and whether pruning explains all pain.
questions: The readings say both that soil must be made ready and that rain and sun do the growing. How are effort and grace divided in the figure, and does Paul's planting and watering divide them the same way?
Some readings speak of barren ground on which nothing grows. How does the vine-dresser's plea for the fig tree bear on that?
Mencius's farmer pulled at his corn to help it. Where have you seen that mistake made in teaching or in raising children?
A reading says the plant most pruned bears the best blossom. When is that a comfort, and when would Ivan Karamazov's protest be the truer word?

outside.why: Jesus tells of a sower whose seed fell by the wayside, on stony places, among thorns and into good ground.
Paul tells a church that they are labourers together with God, and are God's husbandry.
The Song of Songs announces that the winter is past, the rain is over, and the flowers appear on the earth.
James points to the husbandman who waits for the precious fruit of the earth and has long patience for it.
Mencius tells of a man of Song who pulled at his corn to help it grow, and came home tired. What kind of care strengthens roots, and what kind tears them up?
Aristotle holds that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones.
Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful above all things. Is the soil of a child pure of itself, as the reading holds, or is something amiss from the start?
Proverbs passes the field of the slothful and finds it grown over with thorns and nettles.
Hamlet calls the world an unweeded garden that grows to seed, possessed by things rank and gross.
Hosea says: sow in righteousness, reap in mercy, break up your fallow ground.
Isaiah likens God's word to rain and snow that water the earth and make it bring forth and bud.
Moses sings that his doctrine shall drop as the rain and distil as the dew upon the tender herb.
Proverbs asks that understanding be sought as silver and searched for as hid treasures.
Isaiah promises that the one who serves shall be like a watered garden, a spring whose waters fail not.
Jesus explains his own parable in a line the reading takes up: the seed is the word of God.
The psalm pictures a king who comes down like rain upon the mown grass.
Shakespeare gives Iago the saying that our bodies are our gardens, to the which our wills are gardeners. Who tends the soil of the heart in the reading, the self or another?
The psalm says: thou visitest the earth and waterest it, and greatly enrichest it.
Isaiah says that as a garden causes what is sown in it to spring forth, so righteousness shall spring forth.
The Qur’an says that water sent down from the sky flows in each valley according to its measure.
Jesus offers water that becomes in the one who drinks a well springing up into everlasting life.
Isaiah says the wilderness shall be glad, and the desert shall blossom as the rose.
In Luke the good ground is those who hear the word in an honest and good heart and bring forth fruit with patience.
Jesus explains the seed among thorns: the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word.
Ezekiel has God promise to take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh. If sterile soil gives no growth, can the soil itself be changed, and by whom?
The Song of Songs calls the beloved a garden inclosed, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.
In the parable the master forbids pulling up the tares, lest the wheat be rooted up with them. How are thorns and weeds to be cleared from a heart without harm to what is growing?
The dresser of the vineyard pleads for a barren fig tree: let it alone this year also, till I dig about it. Is any soil to be given up as salt-marsh?
Jesus asks whether men gather grapes of thorns or figs of thistles.
Jesus says the seed grows the sower knows not how, first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn.
Paul gives the gardener's law for every life: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Voltaire's Candide ends on the resolve that we must take care of our garden.
Paul says: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
The Preacher says: in the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand.
The psalm promises that they who sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Jesus says that he who is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
Paul asks, what hast thou that thou didst not receive? If some are made of loyal soil, where does their merit lie?
Jesus likens the kingdom to a grain of mustard seed, the least of seeds, which becomes a tree.
The Qur’an likens a good deed to a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.
James asks that the engrafted word be received with meekness, as a stock receives a graft.
The Qur’an likens the faithful to sown corn that sends forth its shoot and rises firm upon its stalk, delighting the sowers.
Isaiah says that the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is his people, and they his pleasant plant.
Jesus sends out workers with the saying that the harvest is great but the labourers are few.
Isaiah pictures God feeding his flock like a shepherd and gently leading those that are with young.
Jesus says the saying is true that one sows and another reaps: you have entered into other men's labours.
Plato holds that the beginning is the most important part, above all with a young and tender thing.
Hosea has God say: I will be as the dew unto Israel; he shall grow as the lily.
Daniel says that they who turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars.
Jesus asks that a light so shine that good works are seen.
Luke says of the child Jesus that he increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
Paul says that he who sows sparingly shall reap also sparingly, and he who sows bountifully, bountifully.
The Qur’an asks of what you cultivate: is it ye who foster it, or are We the Fosterer?
The psalm promises that the righteous shall still bring forth fruit in old age.
The first psalm likens the godly to a tree planted by the rivers, whose leaf shall not wither.
Jesus gives the test that the reading applies to a human life: the tree is known by his fruit.
Jeremiah's tree by the waters spreads its roots by the river and does not cease from yielding fruit.
Isaiah says the comforted shall be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord.
Hebrews calls praise the fruit of our lips, giving thanks to his name.
Jesus says that a branch bears fruit only while it abides in the vine.
Jesus says the Father sends rain on the just and on the unjust.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Paul says that beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image.
Tennyson holds a flower plucked from a wall and sees in it all that God and man is.
Isaiah promises the fir tree instead of the thorn, and the myrtle instead of the brier.
Hannah sings that the Lord raises the poor out of the dust and sets them among princes.
Herbert marvels: who would have thought my shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness?
The lover of the Song says, I am come into my garden.
Jesus says the wind blows where it lists, and so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Blake found the garden of love filled with graves, and Thou shalt not written over a chapel door. What in religion makes the garden of the soul bloom, and what closes it?
Emerson says that all are needed by each one, and nothing is fair or good alone.
Jesus blesses the pure in heart, for they shall see God, as a clear mirror takes the light.
Pope's proverb for the young: just as the twig is bent, the tree's inclined.
Proverbs asks that a child be trained up in the way he should go.
Mark says that Jesus took the children up in his arms and blessed them.
Ezekiel sees trees by a river from the sanctuary, whose leaf shall not fade.
Paul tells Timothy to let no man despise his youth, but to be an example.
The psalm says: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures, he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Jesus says that every branch that bears fruit is purged, that it may bring forth more fruit.
Paul prays that his readers be fruitful in every good work and increase in the knowledge of God.
Paul prays that his readers, being rooted and grounded in love, may comprehend its breadth and height.
Isaiah has God promise to pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground.
The psalmist prays: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
Jesus says that a corn of wheat must fall into the ground and die to bring forth much fruit.
The psalmist's soul thirsts for God in a dry and thirsty land where no water is.
Augustine rests his whole hope on mercy and prays: give what you command, and command what you will.
Isaiah prays: we are the clay, and thou our potter, and we all are the work of thy hand.
Jeremiah watches a potter remake a marred vessel as seemed good to him.
Jesus says the Father is glorified when his disciples bear much fruit.
Shelley asks the wind to drive his dead thoughts over the universe like withered leaves to quicken a new birth.
The psalmist calls himself a green olive tree in the house of God.
Ezekiel foresees desolate land tilled until people say it has become like the garden of Eden.
Jesus says that every plant which his heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.
The psalm says that God sends out his word and melts the ice, and causes the waters to flow.
Thomas à Kempis calls love a great thing that makes every burden light.
The psalmist cries out afflicted and alone, with lover and friend put far from him.
Hebrews says that no chastening seems joyous at the time, but afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness.
Ivan Karamazov says that too high a price is asked for harmony, and hastens to give back his ticket. Does the figure of pruning answer every kind of suffering?
John the Baptist warns that the axe is laid to the root of every tree that brings not forth good fruit.
Milton concludes that God does not need man's work, and that they also serve who only stand and wait. Is a life without visible fruit worthless?
Locke judged that nine parts of ten of what men are, good or evil, comes by their education.
